name: First Bulgarian Empire
summary: A medieval Balkan state founded by the Bulgars under Asparuh. In the 9th–10th centuries it rivalled Byzantium and became a centre of Slavic Christian culture and the Cyrillic script.

location.value: South-eastern Europe; at its height from the Danube Bend to the Black Sea and from the Dnieper to the Adriatic.

terrain.value: The lower Danube plain, the Balkan Mountains and Macedonia.

climate.value: Continental, with cold winters north of the Balkan Mountains.

resources.value: Fertile soils in Moesia, Thrace and Macedonia; salt mines in Transylvania in the 9th century.

disasters.value: Harvests were prone to natural disasters; in 863 earthquakes, a poor harvest and locusts brought famine.

population.value: No reliable estimate; perhaps a few million under Simeon.

urbanisation.value: Capitals at Pliska, then Preslav (from 893); the country remained mostly rural.

migration.value: Bulgars led by Asparuh moved south of the Danube and joined with South Slavs.

economicBase.value: Agriculture (wheat, rye, millet and grapes) and animal husbandry; trade between Byzantium, Central Europe and the Rus’.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade between Byzantium, Central Europe, the Rus’ and the steppes; a trade treaty with Byzantium (716).

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.

moneyAndTax.value: Did not mint coins; taxes were paid in kind, and Byzantium paid tribute at times.

inequality.value: Leading Bulgar noble families held power; peasants bound to noble or church estates increased from the 10th century.

governmentType.value: Ruled by a khan, then a knyaz (prince) after 864, and by tsars (emperors) from 913.

keyRulers.value: Asparuh (founder), Krum, Boris I (converted, 864), Simeon I the Great (893–927), Samuel.

succession.value: The throne passed within the ruling family; in 889 Boris abdicated and a council chose his third son, Simeon, as ruler.

institutions.value: A People’s Council of nobles and the “armed people”; an independent Bulgarian Patriarchate recognised in 927.

stability.value: After Simeon’s death, Peter I (927–969) faced revolts by his brothers and Magyar raids (934–965), but kept peace with Byzantium.

eliteConflict.value: Boris I crushed a revolt of the nobility against Christianisation (866).

armyAndTech.value: Heavy armoured cavalry and siege engines; Krum prepared 5,000 wagons of siege equipment against Constantinople.

majorWars.value: Long wars with Byzantium; Battle of Kleidion (1014).

territoryChange.value: At its height a major power able to compete with Byzantium.

alliancesRivals.value: Rival and sometimes ally of Byzantium (it helped break the Arab siege of Constantinople); allied with the Eastern Franks from 860.

inventions.value: The Cyrillic script was created at the Preslav Literary School.

scienceEducation.value: Literary schools at Pliska–Preslav and Ohrid; Clement taught 3,500 pupils at Ohrid (886–907).

openness.value: Adopted Christianity from Byzantium in 864 but made Old Church Slavonic its official language (893).

communicationTransport.value: Roman roads through the Balkans; boats on the Danube.

religion.value: Worship of Tangra, the Bulgar sky god, and Slavic religions; Christianity from 864.

languageWriting.value: Old Church Slavonic (official from 893); the Glagolitic alphabet, then the Cyrillic script created at Preslav.

artsArchitecture.value: The Madara Rider rock relief (after 705) and the Round Church of Preslav.

socialStructure.value: Monarch, Bulgar noble families, clergy and mostly free peasants living in village communities (zadruga).

sharedIdentity.value: Bulgars and Slavs merged into a Bulgarian nation; Old Church Slavonic helped create a distinct identity.

dailyLife.value: Mostly rural; wheat, rye and millet were staple foods, and meat was important.

neighbours.value: Byzantium, the Franks, Magyars, Pechenegs, Kievan Rus’ and Serbia.

ideasReligions.value: Old Church Slavonic literature spread north and became the common language of much of Eastern Europe.

riseSignals.value: Founded 680–681 after defeating a Byzantine army.

peakPeriod.value: The 9th and 10th centuries, under Simeon I.

declineSignals.value: Invasions by the Rus’ (968–971) and Byzantine wars under Basil II.

outcome.value: Conquered by Byzantium under Basil II in 1018.

sources.value: Byzantine chronicles and inscriptions. Checked against Wikipedia (“First Bulgarian Empire”).
